{{RunningHeader|they|6287|thick}}{{smaller block|With lokkes crulle [curled] as ''they'' were leyd in presse. {{right|''Chaucer'', Gen. Prol. to C. T. (ed. Morris), l. 81.}}}} {{smaller block|''Thei'' dide his comaundement, and com to-geder, ''thei'' thre and two squyres only. ''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 645.}} {{smaller block|''They'' of Italy salute you. Heb. xiii. 24.}} {{smaller block|These are ''they'' which came out of great tribulation. {{right|Rev. vii. 14.}}}} (''b'') Poss. ''their.'' Of or belonging to them: now always preceding the noun, with the value of an attributive adjective. {{smaller block|Pantasilia come pertly with hir pure maidnes, . . . (All ''thaire'' colouris by corse were of cleane white). {{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 10970.}}}} {{smaller block|Some glory in ''their'' birth, some in ''their'' skill, Some in ''their'' wealth, some in ''their'' bodies' force. {{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, xci.}}}} {{smaller block|As if God were so beholden to us for our good deeds as to be bound for ''their'' sakes to forgive us our ill ones! {{right|''Bp. Atterbury'', Sermons, I. ii.}}}} Sometimes formerly used alone, with the value now given to ''theirs.'' {{smaller block|My clothing keeps me full as warm as ''their'', My meates unto my taste as pleasing are. {{right|''Wither'', Motto, C 3 b, repr. (''Nares.'')}}}} (''c'') Poss. ''theirs.'' That which belongs to them: always used without the noun, and having the value of a nominative or an objective. {{smaller block|Belfagor and Belyal and Belssabub als Heyred hem as hyȝly as heuen wer ''thayres.'' {{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 1527.}}}} {{smaller block|This love of ''theirs'' myself have often seen. {{right|''Shak.'', T. G. of V., iii. 1. 24.}}}} {{smaller block|Nothing but the name of zeal appears 'Twixt our best actions and the worst of ''theirs.'' {{right|''Sir J. Denham'', Cooper's Hill.}}}} (''d'') Obj. (acc.), ''them.'' {{smaller block|Bot — if we may with any gyn
Mak ''tham'' to do dedly syn;
Than with ''tham'' wil I wun and wake. {{right|''Holy Rood'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 96.}}}} {{smaller block|For euery off ''thaim'' was full wyse and sage. {{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1624.}}}} {{smaller block|Let him and ''them'' agree it; they are able to answer for themselves. {{right|''Jer. Taylor'', Works (ed. 1835), II. 235.}}}} (''e'') Obj. (dat.), ''them.'' {{smaller block|Give ''them'' wine to drink. {{right|Jer. xxxv. 2.}}}} (''f'') Used for ''those.'' [Now provincial, Eng. and U. S.] {{smaller block|As if between ''them'' twain there were no strife. {{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 405.}}}} {{smaller block|Let ''they'' ministers preach till they 'm black in the face. {{right|''Kingsley'', Westward Ho, xxx.}}}} {{smaller block|Like ''them'' big hotels
Where they shift plates, an' let ye live on smells. {{right|''Lowell'', Biglow Papers, 2d ser., ii.}}}} '''They say''', it is said: ''they'' meaning persons generally. {{smaller block|We must not run, ''they say'', into sudden extreams. {{right|''Milton'', Reformation in Eng., ii.}}}} {{smaller block|''They say'' he will come far ben, that lad; wha kens but he may come to be Sub-Prior himself? {{right|''Scott'', Monastery, xiii.}}}} '''they2†''', ''conj.'' and ''adv.'' A Middle English variant of ''though.'' '''thian-shan''' (thian′shan′), ''n.'' [Named from a range of mountains in central Asia.] A central Asian wild sheep, ''Ovis poli'', notable for the enormous size of the male's horns, which are said to be sometimes 4⅘ feet round the curve, 1½ feet about the base, their tips spreading 3½ feet apart. {{smaller|The animal stands nearly 4 feet high at the shoulder. This sheep is a near relative of the argali and of the Rocky Mountain bighorn. It inhabits high hilly plains, runs with great speed, and is found in flocks of from 30 to 40, but is still very imperfectly known.}} [[File:century v08 p0091 c1f1.png|center|360px]] {{c|Thian-shan (''Ovis poli'').}} '''thiasos''', ''n.'' See ''thiasus.'' '''thiasote''' (thī′a̤-sōt), ''n.'' [< Gr. θιασώτης, a thiasote, < θίασος, a band or company: see ''thiasus.''] A member of or a participant in a thiasus. '''thiasus, thiasos''' (thī′a̤-sus, -sos), ''n.''; pl. ''thiasi'' (-sī). [Gr. θίασος, a band or company (see def.).] In ''Gr. antiq.'', a band or company assembled in honor of a divinity; especially, a Dionysiac band or procession in which men and women took part in character, with boisterous mirth and music, and bearing attributes of the god; sometimes a political, commercial, social, or benevolent association or gild (ἔρανος); specifically, the mythological band of nymphs, mænads, satyrs, etc., forming the personal cortège of Dionysus, and often represented in sculpture and painting. See ''Bacchus.'' '''Thibaudia''' (thi-bâ′di-ä̤), ''n.'' [NL. (Pavon, 1818), named after a French botanist, ''Thibaud'' de Chanvallon, who traveled in the West Indies in 1751.] 1. A genus of gamopetalous plants, type of the tribe ''Thibaudieæ'' in the order ''Vacciniaceæ.'' {{smaller|It is characterized by racemose flowers with small bracts, a short calyx-tube, with five-toothed border, and ten elongated anthers, far surpassed by a membranous extension into straight narrow tubes which open lengthwise by chinks. The 2 species, ''T. floribunda'' and ''T. Pichinchensis'', are natives of the Andes, the United States of Colombia, and Peru. They are shrubs, sometimes with high-climbing stems, bearing alternate evergreen entire leaves with very oblique veins, and numerous pedicelled scarlet flowers in axillary crowded racemes, sometimes tipped with green or yellow. These and also a few species of related genera are known in cultivation as ''thibaudia.''}} 2. [''l. c.''] A plant of this genus. '''Thibaudieæ''' (thi-bâ-dī′ē-ē), ''n. pl.'' [NL. (Bentham and Hooker, 1876), < ''Thibaudia'' + ''-eæ.''] A tribe of gamopetalous plants, of the order ''Vacciniaceæ.'' {{smaller|It is characterized by rather large and usually thick and fleshy or coriaceous flowers with short filaments which are commonly contiguous or connate. It includes 17 genera, of which ''Thibaudia'' is the type: principally mountain shrubs, many of them natives of the Andes.}} '''thibet, Thibetan,''' etc. See ''tibet,'' etc. '''thible''' (thib′l), ''n.'' [Also ''thibel, thivel, theevil, theivil, theedle''; dial. variants of ''dibble''1.] 1. A dibble. ''Halliwell.'' [Prov. Eng.]—2. A stick used for stirring broth, porridge, etc.; a pot-stick. [Prov. Eng. or Scotch.] {{smaller block|The ''thible'' ran round, and the . . . handfuls of meal fell into the water. ''E. Brontë,'' Wuthering Heights, xiii.}} 3†. A slice; a skimmer; a spatula. ''Imp. Dict.'' '''thick''' (thik), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [< ME. ''thicke, thikke, thykke,'' rarely ''thig,'' < AS. ''thicce'' = OS. OFries. ''thikki'' = MD. ''dicke,'' D. ''dik'' = MLG. ''dick'' = OHG. ''dicchi,'' MHG. ''dik, dicke,'' G. ''dick'' = Icel. ''thykkr'' (older forms ''thjokkr'' or ''thjökkr'') = Sw. ''tjok'' = Dan. ''tyk'' (Goth. not recorded); cf. OIr. ''tiug'' (< *''tigu''), thick. Cf. ''tight''1.] I. ''a.'' 1. Having relatively great extent or depth from one surface to its opposite; being relatively of great depth, or extent from side to side: opposed to ''thin.'' {{smaller block|Thre hundred elne was it [the ark] long, Naild and sperd, ''thig'' and strong. {{right|''Genesis and Exodus'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 564.}}}} {{smaller block|Thou art waxen fat; thou art grown ''thick.'' {{right|Deut. xxxii. 15.}}}} {{smaller block|If the Sun is incommodious, we have ''thick'' folding Shutters on the out-Side, and thin ones within, to prevent that. ''N. Bailey,'' tr. of Colloquies of Erasmus, I. 198.}} 2. Having (a specified) measurement in a direction perpendicular to that of the length and breadth; measuring (so much) between opposite surfaces: as, a board one inch ''thick.'' {{smaller block|The walles of the gallery are about two yardes ''thicke'' at the least. ''Coryat,'' Crudities, I. 33. Of Fruits, he reckons the Iacapucaya, like a pot, as big as a great bowle, two fingers ''thicke'', with a couer on it, within full of Chesnuts. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 843.}}}} 3. Having numerous separate parts or individuals set or occurring close together; dense; compactly arranged. {{smaller block|He is the pyes patroun and putteth it in hire ere, That there the thorne is ''thikkest'' to buylden and brede. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), xii. 228.}}}} {{smaller block|We supposed him some French mans sonne, because he had a ''thicke'' blacke bush beard, and the Salvages seldome haue any at all. {{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith's'' Works, I. 184.}}}} {{smaller block|We caught another snow-storm, so ''thick'' and blinding that we dared not venture out of the harbor. {{right|''B. Taylor'', Northern Travel, p. 16.}}}} 4. Having relatively great consistency; also, containing much solid matter in suspension or solution; approaching the consistency of a solid; inspissated: as, ''thick'' cream; ''thick'' paste; often of liquids, turbid; muddy; cloudy. {{smaller block|I can selle Bothe dregges and draffe, and drawe it at on hole, ''Thikke'' ale and thinne ale. ''Piers Plowman'' (B), xix. 398.}} {{smaller block|Forth gusht a stream of gore blood ''thick.'' {{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. i. 39.}}}} {{smaller block|Make the gruel ''thick'' and slab. {{right|''Shak.'', Macbeth, iv. 1. 32.}}}} {{smaller block|At the end, or snout, of the glacier this water issues forth, not indeed as a clear bright spring, but as a ''thick'' stream laden with detritus. ''Huxley'', Physiography, p. 161.}} 5. Heavy; profound; intense; extreme; great. {{smaller block|Moyses sithen held up is hond, And ''thikke'' therknesse cam on that lond. {{right|''Genesis and Exodus'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 3102.}} Bote euer-more Seraphe askes and cries, "Where was Eualac?" the stour was so ''thikke''. {{right|''Joseph of Arimathie'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 18.}}}} {{smaller block|''Thick'' slumber Hangs upon mine eyes. {{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, v. 1. 235.}}}} 6. Obscure; not clear; especially, laden with clouds or vapor; misty; foggy: noting the atmosphere, the weather, etc. {{smaller block|It continued ''thick'' and boisterous all the night. {{right|''Winthrop'', Hist. New England, I. 22.}}}} {{smaller block|Again the evening closes, in ''thick'' and sultry air; There 's thunder on the mountains, the storm is gathering there. {{right|''Bryant'', Count of Greiers.}}}} 7. Mentally dull; stupid; devoid of intelligence: as, to have a ''thick'' head. {{smaller block|He a good wit? hang him, baboon! his wit 's as ''thick'' as Tewksbury mustard. {{right|''Shak.'', 2 Hen. IV., ii. 4. 262.}}}} {{smaller block|What if you think our reasons ''thick'', and our ground of separation mistaken? {{right|''Penn'', Liberty of Conscience, v.}}}} 8. Mentally clouded; befogged; slow, weak, or defective in sense-perception, sometimes in moral perception: as, to be ''thick'' of sight, hearing, etc.: said of persons or of the organs of sense. {{smaller block|The people muddied, ''Thick'' and unwholesome in their thoughts and whispers. {{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iv. 5. 82.}}}} {{smaller block|My sight was ever ''thick''; . . . tell me what thou notest about the field. {{right|''Shak.'', J. C., v. 3. 21.}}}} {{smaller block|I am ''thick'' of hearing, Still, when the wind blows southerly. {{right|''Ford'', Broken Heart, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|A cloudlike change, In passing, with a grosser film made ''thick'' These heavy, horny eyes. {{right|''Tennyson'', St. Simeon Stylites.}}}} 9. Indistinct in utterance; inarticulate; not clear. {{smaller block|He rose and walked up and down the room, and finally spoke in a ''thick'', husky voice, as one who pants with emotion. {{right|''H. B. Stowe'', Oldtown, p. 460.}}}} 10. Abounding; filled; plentifully supplied: followed by ''with'' (formerly ''of'' or ''for''). {{smaller block|The Westerne shore by which we sayled we found all along well watered, but very mountanous and barren, the vallies very fertill, but extreame ''thicke of'' small wood so well as trees. {{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith's'' Works, I. 176.}}}} {{smaller block|His reign [Henry III.'s] was not onely long for continuance, fifty-six years, but also ''thick for'' remarkable mutations happening therein. {{right|''Fuller'', Ch. Hist., III. iv. 24.}}}} {{smaller block|The air was ''thick with'' falling snow. {{right|''Bryant'', Two Travellers.}}}} {{smaller block|She looked up at Eve, her eyes ''thick with'' tears. {{right|''Harper's Mag.'', LXXVIII. 449.}}}} 11. Numerous; plentiful; frequent; crowded. {{smaller block|Thei were so ''thikke'' and so entacched ech amonge other, that mo than a thousand fill in to the river. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), ii. 288.}}}} {{smaller block|These [Oxen and Kine] were . . . exceeding ''thicke'' from the one end of the Market place . . . to the other. {{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 55.}}}} {{smaller block|The brass-hoof'd steeds tumultuous plunge and bound, And the ''thick'' thunder beats the lab'ring ground. {{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xi. 198.}}}} {{smaller block|Lay me, When I shall die, within some narrow grave, Not by itself—for that would be too proud— But where such graves are ''thickest''. {{right|''Browning'', Paracelsus.}}}} 12. Being of a specified number; numbering. [Rare.] {{smaller block|There is a guard of spies ten ''thick'' upon her. {{right|''B. Jonson'', Volpone, i. 1.}}}} 13. Close in friendship; intimate. [Colloq.] {{smaller block|He Could conjure, tell fortunes, and calculate tides, . . . And was thought to be ''thick'' with the Man in the Moon. {{right|''Barham'', Ingoldsby Legends, I. 270.}}}} {{smaller block|Don't you be getting too ''thick'' with him — he 's got his father's blood in him too. {{right|''George Eliot'', Mill on the Floss, ii. 6.}}}} {{smaller|'''Half-thick file.''' See ''file''1.— '''Thick coal,''' a bed of coal in the Dudley district, England, averaging about thirty feet in thickness, "a source of enormous wealth to the district" (''Hull'').— '''Thick focaloid, homeoid, intestine.''' See the nouns.— '''Thick limestone.''' Same as ''scar-limestone.''— '''Thick register.''' See ''register''1, 5 (''b'').— '''Thick squall.''' See ''squall''1.— '''Thick stuff,''' in ''ship-building,'' a general name for all planking above 4 inches in thickness.}} {{smaller block|All the timber, ''thick-stuff,'' and plank to be fresh-cut. {{right|''Laslett'', Timber, p. 76.}}}} {{smaller|'''Thick 'un,''' a sovereign; also, a crown, or five shillings. Sometimes written ''thickun.'' [Cant.]}} {{smaller block|If you like . . . I will send a few ''thickuns'' to bring you . . . to Start. {{right|''Cornhill Mag.'', VI. 648.}}}} {{smaller block|If he feel that it were better for him to quaff the flowing bowl, and he has a drought within him, and a friend or a ''thick 'un'' to stand by him, he is a poor weak cross-grained fool to refuse. {{right|''Percy Clarke'', The New Chum in Australia, p. 143.}}}} {{smaller|'''Through thick and thin,''' over smooth or rough places; with or without obstruction; despite all opposition; unwaveringly; steadily.}}
